extracted.intended_audience: general readers, legal historians, journalists, policy makers and lawyers interested in U.S. obscenity/postal law and the Comstock Act
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the legal standards, prohibitions, historical enforcement practices, and relevant case law and statutes tied to the Comstock Act and related federal obscenity/postal regulations in the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comstock Act statutory prohibitions (textual clauses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act (and related unnumbered subsections quoted on the page) prohibits mailing and circulation of a wide range of items and information: "Every obscene, lewd, lascivious, indecent, filthy or vile article, matter, thing, device, or substance..."; "Every article or thing designed, adapted, or intended for producing abortion, or for any indecent or immoral use..."; and provisions covering materials "which is advertised or described in a manner calculated to lead another to use or apply it for producing abortion, or for any indecent or immoral purpose..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes textual subsections forbidding not only the physical items (obscene works, contraceptives, abortifacients) but also printed material giving information on where or how such things may be obtained or made (e.g., "Every written or printed card, letter, circular, book, pamphlet, advertisement, or notice of any kind giving information, directly or indirectly, where, or how, or from whom, or by what means any of such mentioned matters... may be obtained or made...").

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on mailing information about abortion operations (sealed or unsealed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act's language covers descriptions or instructions on how abortion may be produced and where or by whom any act or operation for procuring abortion will be done, "whether sealed or unsealed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means the statutory prohibition was written to capture not only tangible abortifacients but also instructional or informational communications about procuring abortions, even if enclosed in sealed envelopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical enforcement targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, Comstock-style enforcement targeted pornography, contraceptive equipment, abortion drugs and devices, materials providing descriptions of contraceptive or abortion methods, and materials advertising people with information on or providing birth control or abortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcers particularly targeted advertisements for abortifacients in penny papers and other widely distributed print, and pursued both goods and advertising/informational materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of enforcement scope by private actors (Anthony Comstock)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthony Comstock aggressively sought to expand the reach of the law to include items not obviously sexual (e.g., certain art, medical textbooks) and worked via the Postal Inspection Service and private anti-vice organizations to pursue arrests and seizures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include attempts to include sealed envelopes, international artworks, textbooks for medical students; historically his enforcement produced thousands of arrests and the destruction of large quantities of material ("over 3,600 arrests and the destruction of over 160 tons").

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial limitation via First Amendment jurisprudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Comstock Act remained on the books, "its reach has been somewhat curtailed by the courts based upon first amendment principles." The article cites cases (e.g., Reidel, Roth, Stanley, Hamling, Miller) and notes shifting constitutional limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Supreme Court and federal case law over the 20th century narrowed what the government can criminalize as obscene or nonprotected speech, altering how Comstock-style provisions are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miller test as the modern obscenity standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The article references the Miller Test (Miller v. California, 1973) as central to modern obscenity determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the chunk does not reproduce the three Miller prongs, it signals that the Miller framework (and related Supreme Court decisions) govern whether material is legally 'obscene' for enforcement and prosecution purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial equivalence of descriptive terms to 'obscene'
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts have construed various statutory descriptors — 'obscene, lewd, lascivious, indecent, filthy' — as synonymous with the legal term 'obscene.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: statutory language using many synonyms is interpreted through the established legal concept of 'obscenity' rather than creating distinct categories for each adjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal jurisdiction and intrastate mailings
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that mailings were wholly intrastate is immaterial for prosecution under §1461; the Postal Power Clause does not distinguish between interstate and intrastate matters (citing Smith v. United States).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement under mailing statutes can apply regardless of whether the mailed material crossed state lines; prosecutions rely on Congress's postal power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific federal statutes relevant to mail/obscenity
rubrics_metrics.description: The page references specific statutory provisions used to police mail/obscenity: 18 U.S.C. §1461 (mailing obscene or crime-inciting matter), 18 U.S.C. §1462 (importation or transportation of obscene matters), 39 U.S.C. §3001 (nonmailable matter), and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory sections set the formal legal prohibitions that enforcement and prosecutions invoke; practitioners should consult the exact text and case law interpreting each section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for non-capital offenses (timing constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as otherwise expressly provided by law, no person shall be prosecuted, tried, or punished for any offense not capital unless the indictment is found or the information instituted within five years next after such offense (citing 18 U.S.C. §3282).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural constraint relevant to bringing prosecutions under non-capital obscenity/postal statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern statutory augmentations for child-protection and obscenity
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain sections (18 U.S.C. §§1460, 1465, 1466, 1467, 1468, 1469) were added to chapter 71 by the Child Protection and Obscenity Enforcement Act; 18 U.S.C. §1466A was added by the PROTECT Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These additions reflect Congress's later efforts to target child pornography and related offenses, which interact with and expand the statutory framework that originated with Comstock-era laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial speech and contraception advertising — constitutional protection (Bolger v. Youngs Drug)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bolger v. Youngs Drug Products Corp. (1983) is cited for the proposition that prohibiting mailing of unsolicited contraception advertisements that are accurate and contribute to informed decision-making can violate the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates limits on applying Comstock-style prohibitions to truthful commercial/health information; enforcement must account for constitutional protections of certain informational speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to importation and related legal frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and statutory law also govern importation of obscene matter (see 18 U.S.C. §1462) and other collateral statutes (e.g., tariff/import statutes) referenced on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement can proceed under distinct statutory vehicles (mail, importation, etc.), so legal analysis must identify the applicable statutory hook and the controlling precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive-branch legal analysis on mailing abortion-related drugs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of Legal Counsel produced an opinion titled 'Application of the Comstock Act to the Mailing of Prescription Drugs That Can Be Used for Abortions' (Jan 3, 2023), indicating contemporary executive-branch consideration of whether Comstock-era statutes can reach mailed abortion drugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and enforcement debates over whether the Comstock framework applies to modern medication abortion (e.g., mifepristone) are active; the OLC opinion is an important piece of guidance but not binding judicial authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical legislative intent and enactment context
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act originated as a rider to a postal service consolidation bill in 1872 and was later introduced as a stand-alone Act in 1873 ("Act for the Suppression of Trade in, and Circulation of, Obscene Literature and Articles of Immoral Use").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding legislative history (sponsors, committee actions, motives such as suppression of 'obscene' trade) is relevant for interpreting the statute's original scope and how activists like Anthony Comstock shaped enforcement priorities.
